paths.title: Realtime Systems, Webhooks & External Integrations
paths.description: Build WebSockets, SSE, polling, webhook delivery, third-party clients, retries, signatures, ordering, reconciliation, and integration failure handling.
topics: Polling tradeoffs
Polling is simple and cache-friendly but introduces repeated requests and freshness bounded by the polling interval.
Use polling when update frequency is modest and tune intervals, conditional requests, visibility behavior, and backoff to actual freshness needs.
Server-sent events
SSE provides one-way server-to-browser event streaming over HTTP with automatic reconnection semantics in browsers.
Use SSE for server-push feeds that do not need bidirectional message exchange and define event IDs for resumable delivery when required.
WebSockets
WebSockets provide a long-lived bidirectional channel but move connection lifecycle, backpressure, authorization, and fan-out into application infrastructure.
Authenticate connection establishment and authorize every subscription or command rather than treating an open socket as blanket permission.
Connection state
Realtime clients disconnect, reconnect, sleep, change networks, and miss messages while offline.
Expose connection state, use resumable sequence/version markers, and reconcile current authoritative state after reconnect.
Presence and ephemeral state
Presence, typing indicators, and cursors are usually temporary signals that tolerate loss differently from durable business events.
Keep ephemeral realtime state separate from durable records and expire stale presence without requiring perfect disconnect notifications.
Webhook verification
Incoming webhooks cross a trust boundary and can be spoofed or replayed if signatures and freshness are not validated.
Verify the provider's documented signature over the exact raw payload, enforce timestamp/replay limits, and compare signatures safely.
Webhook delivery
Outgoing webhooks face transient failures, slow receivers, duplicates, redirects, and endpoint compromise.
Deliver asynchronously with bounded retries, signatures, timeouts, delivery logs, and controls to disable persistently failing destinations.
Third-party timeouts
External APIs can hang, throttle, return malformed responses, or change behavior independently of your release cycle.
Set connection/response deadlines, validate schemas, bound response size, and isolate provider failure from core request capacity.
Reconciliation
Events can be delayed, duplicated, missed, or received out of order even when realtime delivery appears reliable.
Maintain a durable source of truth and provide reconciliation jobs or version checks that can repair derived integration state.
Integration ownership
Each external dependency adds credentials, quotas, contracts, incidents, deprecations, and data-sharing responsibilities.
Record owners, scopes, rate limits, data exchanged, fallback behavior, and vendor change procedures for every production integration.

paths.title: Backend Testing, Contracts & CI Verification
paths.description: Use unit, integration, database, contract, security, concurrency, end-to-end, migration, and fault-injection tests to prove server behavior before release.
topics: Unit-test boundaries
Pure domain functions and small services can be tested quickly without starting networks or databases.
Unit-test business rules at their narrowest stable boundary and avoid mocking implementation details that make refactoring unnecessarily expensive.
HTTP integration tests
Route behavior depends on parsing, middleware, auth, status mapping, headers, and serialization that unit tests can miss.
Exercise the actual application server or framework adapter with representative requests and assert status, headers, and response bodies.
Database integration tests
SQL semantics, constraints, transactions, indexes, and migrations are difficult to reproduce faithfully with in-memory mocks.
Run important data tests against the same database engine/version family used in production with isolated reproducible test data.
Contract tests
Consumer/provider contracts catch incompatible API changes when services evolve independently.
Validate published schemas or consumer expectations in CI and treat removed or retyped fields as intentional compatibility decisions.
Authorization tests
Permission defects often appear only when identifiers, tenants, roles, or object ownership differ from the happy path.
Generate negative cases across user, tenant, role, object, and field combinations and keep them required for protected endpoints.
Concurrency tests
Race conditions and uniqueness defects may not appear in sequential tests even when the code looks correct.
Run simultaneous requests around counters, reservations, state transitions, and idempotency to prove database-level invariants.
Migration tests
A migration can succeed on an empty test database but fail on real data, old schemas, long tables, or rollback paths.
Test upgrade from representative prior schema states and validate application compatibility during expand-and-contract phases.
Fault injection
Timeouts, dropped connections, queue duplicates, cache loss, and provider errors reveal whether retry and fallback logic actually works.
Inject controlled dependency failures and assert bounded retries, correct error mapping, cleanup, and preserved invariants.
Test isolation
Flaky tests often share database rows, ports, clocks, queues, or global state across cases.
Give tests isolated resources or deterministic cleanup and avoid order dependence so failures remain reproducible.
CI quality gates
A green unit suite is insufficient if formatting, schema validation, migrations, security checks, integration tests, or production build steps can still fail.
Run the smallest complete required validation matrix on every change and preserve failure logs/artifacts for diagnosis.

paths.title: Observability, Performance & Reliability
paths.description: Operate services using structured logs, metrics, traces, SLOs, timeouts, retries, backpressure, load tests, graceful degradation, and capacity evidence.
topics: Structured logging
Machine-readable logs make it possible to query request, identity, release, outcome, and latency fields without parsing prose.
Use stable fields, correlation IDs, severity levels, and redaction while avoiding full sensitive request or response dumps.
Metrics
Counters, gauges, histograms, and summaries reveal rates, saturation, latency distributions, and error behavior over time.
Measure user-relevant request outcomes plus key resource pools and queue age rather than collecting every internal number without purpose.
Distributed tracing
Traces connect work across services, queues, databases, and external calls through parent/child spans and shared context.
Propagate trace context across synchronous and asynchronous boundaries and annotate spans with safe high-cardinality identifiers only when useful.
Service objectives
SLIs measure user-visible behavior while SLOs define an acceptable target over a time window.
Choose availability, latency, freshness, or correctness indicators that represent real user success and use error budgets to prioritize reliability work.
Timeout budgets
Without deadlines, one slow dependency can consume request capacity and create cascading latency.
Set end-to-end request deadlines and allocate shorter downstream timeouts so enough time remains to fail or recover cleanly.
Retry discipline
Retries multiply traffic during partial outages and can turn a small dependency problem into broad overload.
Retry only transient safe operations, cap attempts, use exponential backoff with jitter, and respect request deadlines and Retry-After.
Circuit breaking and load shedding
When a dependency is unhealthy or capacity is exhausted, failing fast can preserve the rest of the system.
Use bounded queues, admission control, circuit breakers, or degraded modes based on measured failure and saturation signals.
Connection pools
Database and HTTP client pools protect setup cost but oversized pools can overwhelm downstream systems.
Size pools from downstream capacity and concurrency needs, monitor wait time, and always release leased connections.
Load testing
Capacity assumptions need realistic traffic mixes, payload sizes, concurrency, cache state, and dependency behavior.
Load-test representative critical flows, measure saturation and tail latency, and avoid extrapolating from single-endpoint synthetic benchmarks.
Graceful degradation
Optional recommendations, analytics, secondary search, or notifications should not necessarily take core transactions down with them.
Classify dependencies by criticality and design explicit fallback or partial responses for nonessential capabilities.

paths.title: Backend Architecture, Scaling & Deployment
paths.description: Choose modular monolith, services, containers, serverless, scaling, load balancing, discovery, deployment, configuration, and release strategies from actual system constraints.
topics: Modular monolith
A well-structured single deployable can preserve strong module boundaries without distributed-system complexity.
Start with explicit domain modules and extract services only when independent scaling, ownership, isolation, or lifecycle provides clear value.
Service boundaries
Microservice boundaries should align with business capabilities and data ownership rather than arbitrary technical layers.
Give each service a coherent domain responsibility and avoid shared databases that let callers bypass service contracts.
Distributed tradeoffs
Network calls add latency, partial failure, retries, version skew, observability needs, and consistency challenges absent from in-process calls.
Budget distributed complexity explicitly and prefer local calls when independent deployment or isolation does not justify a network boundary.
Horizontal scaling
Multiple stateless replicas increase capacity and resilience only when shared state, jobs, sessions, and database limits are designed for concurrency.
Externalize durable/shared state, use health-aware load balancing, and test behavior during replica addition and termination.
Load balancing
Load balancers distribute requests among healthy instances and may terminate TLS, add forwarding headers, and drain connections.
Configure health checks and connection draining and make the application trust only the known proxy chain.
Container packaging
Containers package application filesystem and runtime dependencies but do not remove the need for secure configuration, health checks, resource limits, or persistent storage design.
Build minimal immutable images, run as non-root where practical, and inject environment-specific secrets/configuration at runtime.
Serverless runtime
Function or managed request runtimes reduce server administration but introduce execution limits, cold starts, connection constraints, and provider-specific lifecycle behavior.
Use serverless for workloads that fit its duration, concurrency, state, and networking model rather than forcing every long-lived process into it.
Deployment strategies
Rolling, blue-green, and canary releases trade capacity, complexity, rollback speed, and version overlap differently.
Choose a release strategy that supports backward-compatible APIs and schema while monitoring the new version before full traffic.
Configuration promotion
Building different artifacts per environment increases the chance that production differs from what was tested.
Build immutable artifacts once and inject environment configuration during deployment whenever the platform and framework support it safely.
Architecture decision records
Important choices lose their rationale over time, causing teams to repeat debates or violate hidden constraints.
Record significant decisions, alternatives, consequences, and review triggers in lightweight version-controlled ADRs.

paths.title: Backups, Recovery, Incidents & Production Operations
paths.description: Prepare backups, restore tests, disaster recovery, incident response, runbooks, maintenance, security patching, data retention, capacity, and post-incident learning.
topics: Backup objectives
Backups need defined recovery point and recovery time objectives rather than an assumption that any backup is sufficient.
Set RPO/RTO by business impact and choose snapshot, continuous log, replica, and offsite strategies that can meet them.
Restore testing
A backup that has never been restored is an unverified hypothesis and may be corrupt, incomplete, encrypted with lost keys, or operationally too slow.
Run scheduled restore drills into isolated environments and verify application-level data integrity, permissions, and required keys.
Disaster recovery
Regional, provider, account, or data-loss disasters require more than restarting the same deployment.
Document dependencies, DNS, secrets, infrastructure, data restore order, and manual decisions needed to rebuild service in the recovery environment.
Incident detection
Incidents should be declared from user impact or credible risk before every technical root cause is known.
Define alert ownership and severity criteria and create an incident channel/timeline early when coordinated response is needed.
Incident roles
Response improves when command, technical investigation, communications, and note-taking responsibilities are explicit.
Assign an incident commander for significant events and separate coordination from deep debugging when team size permits.
Runbooks
Runbooks reduce cognitive load for known operational procedures such as failover, queue drain, credential rotation, or emergency feature disablement.
Keep commands tested, prerequisites explicit, rollback steps included, and links near the alert or dashboard that triggers the runbook.
Patch management
Runtime, OS image, database, framework, and dependency vulnerabilities require supported versions and a repeatable update process.
Track supported release lines, apply security updates promptly according to exposure, and verify patched builds through normal release gates.
Data retention and deletion
Operational copies, logs, caches, backups, and analytics can retain personal or regulated data after primary records are deleted.
Define retention by data class and propagate deletion obligations across secondary stores with auditable procedures.
Capacity planning
Traffic, storage, queue depth, database growth, and third-party quotas can exhaust slowly and predictably before an outage.
Forecast from growth trends and saturation thresholds and validate scaling actions before emergency capacity is needed.
Post-incident learning
Blameless review should identify technical and organizational conditions that allowed the incident and improve detection, prevention, or recovery.
Build a factual timeline, distinguish root/contributing factors, assign concrete follow-up owners, and verify corrective actions are completed.
